title: What has changed
hookLine: look at who you were on day one
tomorrow: the family finishes the whole book. what does Dadi do first?

cards: Every December the apps send a recap: your year in songs, in steps, in photos. This one arrives in person. A grandmother, home from knee surgery, leg up on a pillow, studies her granddaughter and says: you've changed.
You pray on time now. You listen longer before you answer. And the granddaughter squirms.
Part of her wants to say thank you. Part of her wants to say no, not really. So which is it?
Should you count your own progress, or is counting your own good a trap?

teach.b: Both answers live inside the tradition. First, the case for looking. The Qur'an says change is real, and starts inside: God does not change the condition of a people until they change what is in themselves.
And a hadith in Tirmidhi says that whoever is glad at their good deed and sad at their bad one is a believer. Gladness at your good isn't pride; it's a sign of a living heart.

The Qur'an even tells the Prophet ﷺ, after reminding him how far he's come: "Therefore of the bounty of thy Lord be thy discourse." Speak of the gift. Look back, see what's different, and say whose gift it was.

Now the case for caution. The Qur'an also says: don't claim purity for yourselves; God knows best who is truly mindful of Him. Scholars name a quiet danger, 'ujb, admiring yourself, the good deed that turns into a mirror.
And the Prophet said deeds are judged by how they end. A summit isn't a finish line. Someone who stops to admire the view can forget there's a way down, and a next climb.
Here's what both sides share, and it's worth telling a friend tonight: neither says you haven't changed.
They disagree about where to put your eyes. One says look at the gift and say thank you. The other says look at the road still ahead.
A grandmother on a couch can hold both.

how: Muslims practice muhasaba, taking account of oneself, often at night or at the year's turn: thanking God for good that has grown and asking forgiveness for what hasn't, while scholars warn against self-admiration ('ujb).

o: proof that you've reached the end
an honest look at how you've grown
a list of the rules you've broken

games.q: which side said it — tap the pairs.
p: change starts in what is in themselves
glad at your good is a sign of faith

s: in a hadith, being glad at your own good deed is a sign of faith
Tirmidhi 2165: glad at the good, sad at the bad.
the Qur'an says people can't really change
13:11: God changes a people's condition when they change what is in themselves.
a hadith says deeds are judged by how they end

games.q: your friend writes down every good deed each night and adds a gold star. a cousin calls it risky. give the cautious side's best case.
o: the Qur'an says don't claim purity for yourselves; God knows best who is mindful.
good deeds should be hidden even from the angels who record them.
writing things down is a modern habit, so it can't belong to faith.
games.why: 53:32 and the warning against 'ujb are the cautious side's strongest ground. the other side has 13:11 and Tirmidhi 2165: being glad at your good is a sign of faith.

practice: Take a scrap of paper and write one sentence: one thing that's different about you since you started this path. Under it, write who or what helped it change.
Then turn the paper over and sit with the blank side until the time is up: that's the part still being written.

wordCard.voice: What has changed: the honest look back, held with thanks for the gift and an eye on the road ahead.

orig.note: Arabic: the self, the soul; 13:11 speaks of what is 'in themselves' (bi-anfusihim).

carryVoice: Your line: who I am now, given, and not finished. Twelve of fifteen, three to go.

sources.q: Therefore of the bounty of thy Lord be thy discourse.
